slides: That's the area of triangles. Just one more small tip to finish.

slides.say: A median of a triangle cuts it into two triangles with the same area. Remember, a median goes from a vertex to the middle of the opposite side. Here's a triangle, A B C. It doesn't have to be special. Not equilateral, not isosceles, just any triangle.
Draw the median from A. It goes to D, the middle of B C, so B D and D C are equal.
Now we have two triangles, A B D and A D C. Their bases, B D and D C, are equal.
And they have the same height. Drop the altitude from A to the line B C. This one altitude is the height of both triangles. For the triangle on the right, it falls outside, but that doesn't matter.

Same base, same height, so the same area. For example, if B C is ten and the height is six, each half has a base of five, so its area is five times six over two, fifteen. And the whole triangle is ten times six over two, thirty, twice as much.
Careful, the same area doesn't mean the same shape. These two triangles look very different. They don't have the same shape, and they don't have the same side lengths. Only their areas are equal.
The same idea works when the top vertex moves along a line that's parallel to the base. Here the base is B C, and the dashed line is parallel to it.
at: Here the base is B C

slides.say: Put the top vertex at the left, in the middle, or far to the right. The base stays the same, and the height is always the distance between the two parallel lines, so it doesn't change either. So all these triangles have the same area.

slides: So whenever you see a median, you automatically know that it cut the triangle into two triangles with equal areas. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next video.
